author: chokobole
body:
`poly1305_test`'s differential sweep runs eight `B = 1` calls per length, which
reads like the batch-axis anti-pattern the conventions page warns about and so
invites a rewrite into one `B = 8` call. That rewrite was proposed. Measuring it
first says it does not pay, so this records why at the loop instead of doing it.

## Why it stopped paying

It was a real fix once. Before #88 retired the 13-bit limb field, every `mac()`
call walked a ten-limb layout op-by-op and a repeat at a fixed shape cost full
price — which is exactly what proved dispatch dominated. A registered field
dtype collapsed that to one field multiply per block, and compilation is now the
whole cost:

| msg len | B=1 first | B=1 repeat | B=8 first |
|---------|-----------|------------|-----------|
| 1       | 513.4     | 2.31       | 544.4     |
| 15      | 17.4      | 2.11       | 22.6      |
| 16      | 9.8       | 2.07       | 8.3       |
| 17      | 185.9     | 2.12       | 229.4     |
| 64      | 194.7     | 2.18       | 202.6     |
| 70      | 214.2     | 2.13       | 218.4     |

(ms, CPU leg.) A first call at a shape runs 8-544ms; a repeat at that same shape
runs ~2.1ms.

**Batching removes dispatches, not shapes.** The six lengths straddle the block
boundary on purpose, so they stay six distinct compilations either way. The
rewrite buys the 42 repeats — ~90ms of a ~1.3s test — and hands it back at the
compiler, where the `B = 8` graphs cost 1226ms to build against 1135ms for the
`B = 1` ones.

I also ran the two arms end to end, and both passes favoured the loop. Those
numbers are not quoted here: a sibling lane held the box at loadavg 17-24, and
per the sizing rule's own reasoning a contaminated wall clock is not a figure.
The ratio table is what carries the conclusion — at 100x separation, load noise
cannot invert it.

`Poly1305BatchTest` already covers the batch axis directly, and the conventions
page's batch-axis rule is about the seams, where there is no scalar entry point
to implement — not about a test's input sweep.

## The second commit

Writing this up, the natural home looked like `docs/reference/conventions.md`.
It is not: that page opens by saying the rules every FRX consumer shares are
**not** repeated there, because a copy per repo is how they drift apart. A
compile-versus-dispatch rule is one of those shared rules. But the paragraph
never says where they *are*, so the reader who needs one has nowhere to go —
hash-frx's page already links zorch for exactly this. The second commit matches
it. The shared rule itself is filed against zorch.

## Testing

`bazel test //enc_frx/chacha/testing:poly1305_test` passes (3.4s). Comment-only
change to the test plus a prose line in docs — no behaviour touched.

body:
Two changes: the app now says why a ticker is listed at all, and the sections that were handset layouts in a desktop window get an edge and the width.

## The screen cut-off

Every published row is in the file because its change reached a cut-off the run applied — the `threshold` column each per-window table carries — and the app never said so, which left the lists looking like an unexplained selection of tickers.

The cut-off is per window, not global: both files screen at 10% for 7 days and 1 month, and 25% from 3 months out, so a single app-wide constant would have been wrong.

It now rides along on `StockRow` (and on `ConsistentStock`, from its own `threshold_shortest_window` column), and `MarketDatabase.threshold()` reads the per-window value once and caches it.

On screen:

| Place | What it says |
|---|---|
| Detail screen, under the price | "Its 7 day change of +117.9% is past the 10.0% cut-off this screen applies, by 107.9 points." |
| Detail → Metrics | `Screen cut-off` and `Margin over cut-off` |
| Detail → Windows | a **Cut-off** column beside Change |
| List footer | `107 stocks · cut-off 10.0%` |
| Consistent rows | `shortest window · 10.0%` |
| Both info sheets | where the number comes from |

Switching window pills switches the rule with it, which is what makes the stricter long-window screens visible.

A cut-off is only claimed when the file publishes one. An older file without the column, and a table that somehow mixes cut-offs, both fall back to saying nothing rather than describing rows with a rule that was not applied.

## Framed desktop sections

Settings, Analysis and Reports were handset layouts dropped into a desktop window: cards floating on a page background with no edge of their own, capped at 980px so a third of the window stayed empty beside them.

- `PageFrame` puts the same bordered surface the tables use around those three sections, keeping each screen's app bar as its header band.
- The readable-width cap goes to 1280.
- Settings deals its sections into three columns from 1120px, two from 820, one below that.

## Testing

- `flutter analyze` — clean
- `flutter test` — 145 passing, 7 skipped (new: the per-window read and its cache, a legacy file without the column, a mixed table, the five places the cut-off reaches the screen, the frame and its width, the three-column deal)

author: paralin
body:
A message-kind field whose reference resolves to a type declared in another .pb.go file of the same proto package fell through to the goscript/protobuf-ts-binding:unresolved diagnostic, because field resolution only consulted the bound message names of the current file. The Mercury hosted compile gate hit this on mercury_game.WorldSnapshot and mercury_game.WorldEvent referenced from sdk/game/world_storage.proto: same package, different file, connected by a proto import.

The binding pass now indexes the bound messages of every binding file in a package-wide registry. When a same-package field reference misses the current file's names, resolution falls back to that registry and qualifies the sibling binding's message class with a dedicated side-effect import of the sibling .pb.js, minted once per file through the existing unique import alias mechanism. The fallback is fail-closed: a reference that matches no bound message in the package still reports unresolved.

Exact same-file bindings, cross-package import-alias references, and digit-camel capitalization divergence keep their existing resolution paths. Adds TestProtobufTypeScriptBindingResolvesSamePackageCrossFileRefs, which compiles a two-file same-package proto pair with pointer and slice-of-pointer fields referencing messages from the sibling file.

author: monkopedia-coder
body:
Addresses #261, scoped to items 1 and 3 of the triage split. **Stacked on #265** (issue #258)
— based on that branch, so this diff shows only the test-reporting change. It does not depend
on #265 functionally; the branches were worked serially.

`kotlin.test` has no portable skip, so a guarded test reports as **passed** while asserting
nothing. Every platform guard now routes through `skipUnsupported(test, reason)`, which emits
a `KSRPC-SKIP` marker.

## The number nobody had

The marker lands in the result XML's `system-out`, on browser targets included, so the no-ops
are countable:

```
grep -rho 'KSRPC-SKIP [a-zA-Z]*' build/test-results/<task> | sort | uniq -c
```

| platform | tests reported | no-ops | share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| jvm | 621 | 51 | 8.2% |
| linuxX64 | 573 | **85** | 14.8% |
| js | 388 | 48 | 12.4% |
| wasmJs | 395 | 48 | 12.2% |

Between one test in twelve and one in seven asserts nothing, depending on target. The
distribution matches `platformSupportedTestTypes()` where you would expect — `linuxX64` skips
`WEBSOCKET` and `SERVICE_WORKER` 39 times each, jvm skips `SERVICE_WORKER` 40 times — with one
detail the issue's table does not predict: **jvm also skips `testWebsocketPath` 4
times**, and every platform skips `SERIALIZE`/`PIPE` a few times. Those come from per-class
`supportedTypes` overrides rather than from the platform, so they are the cases where a class
opted out of a capability its platform does have. Worth a look on its own; not touched here.

## Two corrections to the issue

**The guard count is 14, not 6.** #261's comment records
`ServiceWorkerTest.kt:32, 44, 131` in each of `jsTest` and `wasmJsTest`. There are seven per
file — lines 32, 44, 55, 76, 96, 131, 145 — so 14 total. All are routed here.

**One of them already had a marker.** Line 76 read:

```kotlin
if (!hasWindow()) {
    println("No window found")
    return@runBlockingUnit
}
```

so the pattern had been half-invented already, in one place, undocumented and inconsistent
with its six neighbours. It now uses the same helper.

## What I got wrong on the way, since it changes the conclusion

I first wrote the helper's doc claiming the marker was *not* recoverable from the result XML —
reasoning from the observation that 77 of 79 wasm XML files have an empty `system-out`, and
that the two non-empty ones contain library exception text with zero `println` calls in their
sources. That inference was wrong. `system-out` was empty because nothing was printing.
Measured after wiring the marker up: 15 files carry it. So item 3 of the triage scope is fully
achievable rather than best-effort, and the doc now says so.

It is *not* in the Gradle console output for browser runs — only in the XML.

## Item 2 (383 vs 379) — reframed, not resolved

The issue proposes `hasWindow()` differing between a local Chromium and the runner's as "the
obvious candidate" for four tests that "were not merely no-ops but were not generated at all".

**`hasWindow()` cannot produce that symptom.** It is evaluated inside the test body, so a test
it guards is still generated and still counted — that is the entire defect this issue is
about. It can change how many tests *assert*, never how many *exist*.

What can produce it: the suite is nondeterministic in how many tests it reports at all. Three
runs of `wasmJsBrowserTest` against one unchanged commit gave 395, 395 and **388**
([measured on #255](https://github.com/Monkopedia/ksrpc/issues/255#issuecomment-5391129837)).
That is a 7-test swing on one machine with no code change, which is larger than the 4-test gap
item 2 is trying to explain across two machines. The js count is also 388 today against the
383 recorded in August, so the original pair is stale relative to this tree.

I did **not** repeat the js suite to check whether it varies the same way, and I did not
compare against a runner — that half still needs one. But the local-vs-runner framing should
not be assumed before same-machine variance is ruled out.

## Verification

- `ktlintCheck`, `licenseCheckForKotlin` — pass
- `jvmTest` — pass
- `:ksrpc-test:linuxX64Test` — pass
- `:ksrpc-test:jsBrowserTest` — 388 tests, 12 failures, all the #255 signatures, unchanged
- `:ksrpc-test:wasmJsBrowserTest` — 395 tests, 18 failures, unchanged from the #265 branch it
  is stacked on

No test's pass/fail behaviour changes: the guards return exactly where they returned before,
one line earlier.

---

**Review follow-up (`8bdaeeb`).** Two findings from the cross-repo review, both verified before
fixing and both real:

- The documented breakdown recipe used `[a-zA-Z]*`, which excludes `_`, so all seven
  `wasmServiceWorkerConnection_*` guards collapsed into one bucket. A report that looks complete
  while merging distinct things — the exact defect this mechanism exists to expose, shipped in
  the doc-comment advertising it. Now `[A-Za-z0-9_]*`.
- `testHttpPath()` was labelled `testHttpPassthrough` and `testWebsocketPath()` was labelled
  `testWebsocketPassthrough`, copied from the issue's prose rather than the Kotlin symbols, so
  grepping either real function name found nothing.

Totals unchanged (jvm still 51), since both are naming rather than behaviour. Verified breakdown
after the fix: `testServiceWorkerPassthrough` 40, `testWebsocketPath` 4, `testHttpPath` 3,
`testSerializePassthrough` 3, `testPipePassthrough` 1.

Also took the reviewer's denominator point: the KDoc now says the 395 is not stable and points
at #255, so a reader hitting a different number has an in-code pointer rather than only the PR
description, which will not outlive the merge.

## Summary

- exclude `*.test.ts` and `*.test.tsx` from the compiled-tree source mtime scan
- exclude only a workspace-root `test/` tree, matching workspace TypeScript configuration
- keep nested emitting paths such as `debug-view/test/input-probe.ts`, `*.spec.ts`, and `contest/` in the stale-source guard

A newer test file can never be made older than `out/` by `yarn compile` because it emits no output. The old guard therefore refused forever after a test-only edit. A blanket `test/` exclusion would hide real compiled modules, so the path rule is segment-exact and workspace-root-only.

## What this PR does

Rejects validated `@`-file reads when the approved or reopened file identity has an unverifiable inode value such as `0`, instead of treating `{ dev, ino: 0 }` as a usable identity match.

## Why it's needed

Issue #8227 points out that validated file reads rely on `(dev, ino)` identity checks after approval. On filesystems where inode identity is unavailable or reported as `0`, matching on inode `0` is vacuous: multiple files can share the same placeholder identity, so the validation step cannot prove the reopened file is the one the user approved. The new guard fails closed for unverifiable inode identities while keeping the existing identity checks for normal filesystems.

## Reviewer Test Plan

### How to verify

Run the targeted read-many-files tests, the core typecheck, and Prettier on the touched files.

### Evidence (Before & After)

Before: a regression test with mocked `fs.stat()` / file-handle `stat()` returning `ino: 0` would still include the validated file content. After: the same path is omitted from successful file content and returned as a visible read error explaining that the validated identity is unavailable on this filesystem.

### Tested on

|     OS     | Status |
| :--------: | :----: |
|  🍏 macOS  | ✅ tested |
| 🪟 Windows | ⚠️ not tested locally; covered by CI |
|  🐧 Linux  | ⚠️ not tested locally; covered by CI |

### Environment (optional)

Local Node/npm workspace on macOS.

## Risk & Scope

- Main risk or tradeoff: Low to moderate; filesystems that cannot provide verifiable inode identity now fail closed for validated reads rather than allowing an unverifiable match.
- Not validated / out of scope: Windows native filesystem manual testing; the inode-zero behavior is covered with mocked stat results.
- Breaking changes / migration notes: None expected; this only affects validated reads whose identity cannot be verified.

## Linked Issues

Refs #8227. This handles the inode-zero fail-closed behavior; Windows runner coverage and broader platform policy remain separate follow-up scope.

## What does this PR do?

Fixes #93557 — a DM opened **while the gateway is running** was never discovered when the WebSocket transport was active: `_websocket_loop()` relied on kind-44100 membership events alone, and relays have been observed materializing new DMs in `dms list`/`channels list` without ever emitting that event. The conversation stayed invisible until the next WS reconnect. The poll transport was unaffected (`_poll_loop()` re-runs discovery every `_DM_DISCOVERY_EVERY` sweeps).

## Related Issue

Fixes #93557

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)
- [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality)
- [ ] 🔒 Security fix
- [ ] 📝 Documentation update
- [x] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage)
- [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub)

## Changes Made

`plugins/platforms/buzz/adapter.py`:

- Extract `_refresh_conversation_subscriptions(websocket, subscriptions)` — one idempotent discovery+subscription path shared by both transports. It re-runs `_discover_dms(seed=False)` and subscribes the live socket to any watched conversation missing from the subscription map. Keying on what the socket *actually covers* (instead of the old before/after diff over `_channel_state`) makes repeated refreshes and reconnects safe from duplicate REQs.
- Bound each `recv()` at `poll_interval * _WS_REDISCOVERY_EVERY` (5 quiet windows ≈ 20s at defaults) instead of `async for raw in websocket`; on timeout, run the refresh and continue receiving.
  - **recv() is never cancelled mid-flight**: the timeout can only fire after a fully idle window, so refresh awaits cannot race inbound frames; anything delivered during a refresh stays buffered in the transport and is consumed by the next `recv()`.
  - Transport errors surface to the existing reconnect/backoff path as `ConnectionError("receive failed: …")`.
- Frame decoding moves verbatim into `_handle_websocket_message()` so the pump stays readable; routing for EVENT / membership / CLOSED / NOTICE frames is unchanged.
- Freshly discovered conversations dispatch from their beginning, matching the poll transport's documented mid-run behavior.

`tests/gateway/test_buzz_adapter.py`:

- Refresh subscribes a newly discovered conversation; idempotent no-op when already covered.
- Membership-event path routes through the same helper (behavioral parity between transports).
- Loop integration tests via a fake `websockets.connect`: quiet socket triggers periodic rediscovery (3 refreshes observed, same socket object + live subscription map), and frames flow through the real decoder/subscription routing with the refresh firing after traffic resumes-then-quiets.

## How to Test

1. `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/gateway/test_buzz_adapter.py tests/gateway/test_buzz_websocket.py -q` → 32 passed.
2. Live check on a self-hosted relay with WS established: open a new DM to the agent mid-session → it dispatches within ~`poll_interval × _WS_REDISCOVERY_EVERY` without any reconnect or membership event (previously: never, until reconnect).

body:
**P6 closes, and the row's own finding was wrong. That is the more useful half.**

The 2026-08-23 rule census reported three architecture fitness functions — `check_wiring_contract`, `check_negative_control`, `check_test_authenticity` — as appearing *"only in `.github/workflows/validate.yml`"*, making **G-V14** a `BLOCK`-tier guardrail with 3 of its 4 fitness functions unreachable locally.

**They were never CI-only.** All four are listed in `scripts/local-gate-set.txt`, and the pre-push hook is **data-driven off that file**: it reads the lines and runs each script, **naming none of them**. A grep for a script name therefore finds only `validate.yml` and reads as CI-only — while the gate has been blocking every push all along.

**A name-grep answered a question about behaviour.** That is the false-absence class this project logs most often, and here it produced a `BLOCK`-tier alarm about a gate that was working.

## What was genuinely unmet

G-V14 is *"satisfied by the project's verification command (test script, `make check`, pre-commit) invoking them"*. The closest thing to that is `scripts/gates.sh` — the command a builder runs after a change. **It ran four gates against fifteen in the set, and read a different list from CI and pre-push.**

`gates.sh` is now driven off `local-gate-set.txt`, the same single source as CI and the pre-push hook, so the three surfaces cannot drift apart again. `check_gate_parity.py` already asserts CI ⊆ gate-set; this closes the last surface reading a different list.

**Result: `gates.sh` reports ALL PASSED 18/18, up from 4.**

## Two carve-outs, stated in the code rather than discovered later

- **`check_coverage_floor` is DEFERRED there, with its reason printed.** Its input is a fresh `coverage.json`, produced by the pytest-with-coverage step CI and pre-push run and this command deliberately does not (plain pytest is seconds; coverage is minutes). Running it here would either read a **stale** `coverage.json` — green on numbers nobody just measured — or fail on a precondition the builder did not break. It still blocks at pre-push and in CI.
- **An absent gate set is not a failure.** A consumer project running the shipped wrapper has no `plugins/mycelium/scripts`; failing them for that is a defect they cannot have. A gate **named in an existing set but missing on disk** stays a hard failure — a gate set that quietly shrinks reports green while checking less.

## Caught by its own test suite

The first version of this change failed `test_gates_wrapper.sh`, whose fixture is a bare temp repo with no `plugins/` — exactly the consumer case. The test existed before the change and did its job.

## Verification

`gates.sh` 18/18 · 1106 python tests, 91.07% coverage · per-file floor all 51 scripts ≥70% · 61 bash test files · full pre-push template-integrity suite.

author: szavadsky
body:
## Problem

Markdown streaming re-lexes the entire tail on every inert delta (text append), even though only the last row changes. For long paragraphs this is the dominant cost (#9048 perf evidence).

## Approach

When a transient streaming frame's last content row came from a paragraph, an append-only same-line delta re-renders ONLY that row — a splice of the re-wrapped grown row onto the previous frame's cached rows — instead of re-lexing the whole tail. The splice is **byte-identical to a cold full render at every frame** (the new text shows every frame — no lag). On any hazard that could change the token shape, the fast path disarms with a full-relex fallback.

## Hazard gates (every gate has a load-bearing test)

| Gate | Disarms when |
|------|--------------|
| Line-start block-kind | Grown line starts ATX heading, blockquote, list marker, HR (`*+-─━═–—=`), or ref-def |
| Seam URL/email | Raw or decoded tail contains a protocol head, `www.`, or email prefix |
| Entity seam | Partial or complete numeric entity at row end (`&am`, `#`, `#`) |
| Decoded-tail swatch | Entity decodes to `#` mid-row (`#ab` → `#ab` → swatch lead) |
| Decoded-tail run-end | Entity decodes to trailing space (` ` → wrap-trim shift) |
| Cross-seam pair re-pair | Delta opens `*`/`~`/`` ` ``/`[` when row ends with the matching close char |
| Image marker | Row ends `!` + delta starts `[` (image completion across seam) |
| Underscore flanking | Delta starts/ends `_` after a word char |
| Open inline construct | Delta's inline token stream holds an unclosed delimiter |
| Wrap-trim/escape/run-end | Row tail ends in whitespace, backslash, or partial hex swatch |
| Signature/width/reset | bgColor, theme, width mismatch, or cache flip |

## Byte-identity contract

Every frame of every reveal is asserted byte-identical to a cold full render of the same prefix. A shared `assertByteIdentityEveryFrame` helper (step-1 reveal through one transient instance) and a 2-frame `assertSpliceParts` helper (explicit seam-staging for multi-char deltas that step-1 cannot reach) cover every gate. A splice-engagement counter (`fastTailSplices`) asserts the fast path actually runs — a regression that silently disarms (e.g. an over-broad gate matching all ASCII) is caught.

## Benchmark (median-of-3, interleaved, width=100, identity theme)

| Case | Frames | Plain p50 | B+ p50 | Engage% | Saves% |
|------|--------|-----------|--------|---------|--------|
| pureProse:32KB@24 | 1365 | 4.42ms | 0.79ms | 86.4% | **72.0%** |
| emphasis:32KB@24 | 1365 | 643.93ms | 1.30ms | 58.7% | **57.4%** |
| tight:32KB@24 | 1365 | 17.91ms | 11.64ms | 22.1% | **32.6%** |
| tightStream:32KB@24 | 1365 | 293.75ms | 75.65ms | 33.5% | **21.6%** |
| tight:128KB@72 | 1820 | 65.71ms | 51.02ms | 12.4% | **16.5%** |
| singleParagraph:32KB@24 | 1365 | 35.50ms | 32.75ms | 0.0% | 10.7% |
| realistic:8KB@24 | 341 | 0.42ms | 0.31ms | 21.7% | 10.1% |
| realistic:32KB@24 | 1365 | 0.46ms | 0.39ms | 22.9% | 5.5% |
| realistic:128KB@72 | 1820 | 0.56ms | 0.57ms | 13.4% | 2.1% |
| refdef:32KB@24 | 1364 | 0.32ms | 0.32ms | 22.8% | -0.7% |

**Notes**: `tight:128KB@72` rerun under quiet load (loadavg <1); first run under load 84 showed −62.3% (scheduler noise — p90 282→494ms). `refdef` is net-neutral (the fast path's gate overhead ≈ the skipped lex at this size). Run-level styled streams (thinking traces, colored assistant content) disarm entirely — the gain materializes for unstyled content.

## Tests (29 deterministic, zero wall-clock)

- 25 byte-identity + seam-fixture tests (step-1 reveal + 2-frame splice for every gate)
- 3 gate unit tests (line-start hazard: prose-safe, block-marker/HR-fire, ref-def)
- 1 splice-engagement assertion (counter > 0 on prose reveal)

## Review history

Successor to closed PR #9509, addressing all its review threads. Five rounds of adversarial review (fresh reviewer each round) resolved: cross-seam pair re-pairing (`*`/`~`/`` ` ``), image marker (`!`+`[`), box-drawing HR chars, entity-decoded swatch lead, char-class range bug (killed the fast path), dead decoded-URL arm, and splice-engagement test coverage.

body:
Fixes #7.

**Root cause:** `mise run install` used `uv pip install`, which ignores `uv.lock` and re-resolves from `pyproject.toml`. Two unbounded constraints drift:

| Dep | `uv.lock` | Actually installed | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mcp>=1.27.1` | 1.27.1 | 2.0.0 (2026-07-28) | test collection fails |
| `ruff>=0.15.0` | 0.15.14 | 0.16.4 | 95 lint errors |

The ruff one is structural - `select = ["ALL"]` picks up every rule a new release adds, so any ruff release can break a fresh clone.

**Fix:** one line - `run = "uv sync --locked"`.

`--locked` over bare `uv sync` because bare silently rewrites `uv.lock` when `pyproject.toml` changes. `uv lock --check` passes on main, so the lockfile is unchanged here.

**Tested**
fresh clone, `rm -rf .venv && mise run install && mise run check`:

before: `Found 95 errors` / `271 tests collected, 1 error`
after: `All checks passed!` / `Success: no issues found in 44 source files` / `270 passed, 9 skipped`

macOS/arm64, Python 3.12.14 and 3.11.5.

The mcp 2.x direction question (support it, or bound to `<2`?) is in #7, not here.

## Summary

Allow geo rule-sets and subscriptions to download without an active VPN when the kill switch is disabled.

When the kill switch is enabled, downloads require an active VPN connection.

## Changes

- Apply the same network policy to:
  - Regional geo databases
  - Steam and Telegram rule-sets
  - Subscription updates
- Allow direct downloads when the kill switch is disabled.
- Block manual downloads when the kill switch is enabled and VPN is disconnected.
- Keep automatic updates pending until the VPN connects.
- Download missing service rule-sets immediately when enabling service routing.
- Preserve newly added subscriptions when their initial fetch is blocked.
- Log a separate VPN retry hint after failed downloads without a VPN.
- Report service rule-set updates and partial failures instead of silently discarding them.

## Behavior

| Kill switch | VPN | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Disabled | Disconnected | Download directly |
| Disabled | Connected | Download through the active connection |
| Enabled | Disconnected | Block manual downloads; automatic updates wait |
| Enabled | Connected | Download through VPN |

Manual operations blocked by the kill switch must be retried after connecting. Due automatic updates start on the next daemon tick after the VPN becomes connected.

author: inureyes
body:
## Summary

An unusable `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN` surfaced as git's `remote: Invalid username or token` at the very end of the job, after it had cloned the tap, downloaded four release assets, rewritten the formula and committed the result. This adds a step that checks the token against the GitHub API before the clone, and says what is actually wrong.

The v0.26.0 release is the case that motivated it. Run [32688718265](https://github.com/lablup/all-smi/actions/runs/32688718265) failed on the push with that message, and the message pointed at neither the secret nor which of the two places it can be set from.

## What the check distinguishes

git reports all four of these identically. The API does not.

| Result | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| 401 | expired or revoked |
| 403 | refused for this repository, usually SSO authorization or an organization resource restriction |
| 404 | the token was never granted the tap; a fine-grained token reports 404 for a repository outside its access list |
| 200, `permissions.push` false | read-only, needs `Contents: write` |

The write bit is asserted separately because a 200 only proves the token can read a public repository, which any token can.

## Why git could not have told us

A local reproduction settled this rather than leaving it as an assumption. Cloning the tap anonymously and pushing through the **same credential helper** with a deliberately bogus token produces output byte-identical to the real failure:

```
remote: Invalid username or token. Password authentication is not supported for Git operations.
fatal: Authentication failed for 'https://github.com/lablup/homebrew-tap.git/'
```

Removing the helper produces a different message (`could not read Username`), which is what proves the helper fired and the value was the problem. So the git error distinguishes neither the cause among the four above, nor a bad value from a bad mechanism. That second ambiguity cost real time here: the credential-helper push added in #318 was under suspicion, and it turned out to be innocent.

## Every message names where the secret is read from

Two places can define it and the narrower one wins: an environment secret on `packaging` shadows an organization secret of the same name. Rotating the organization copy while a stale environment copy exists changes nothing in this job. That is exactly what had happened, so the messages say it rather than leaving the next person to find it.

## The security trade, stated rather than glossed

This is the second step the token is exposed to, where the note on the push step says one. The comment records the trade: one more step holding the credential, in exchange for a failure that arrives before anything is mutated and that names the repair.

The token still reaches no argv, no file, and no remote url. `printf` is a bash builtin, so no process on the runner carries it in its command line, and the header goes to curl on stdin for the same reason the push step keeps it out of `-c http.extraheader`.

## Test plan

- [x] YAML parses; step order is `Determine version tag` -> `Verify the tap token` -> `Clone Homebrew tap repository`
- [x] The emitted bash extracted from the parsed workflow and run against the real GitHub API on three branches:
  - empty value -> exit 1, names the two secret locations
  - bogus token -> 401 branch, exit 1
  - token with write access to `lablup/homebrew-tap` -> `Tap token accepted`, exit 0
- [x] `jq` is already used by this workflow, so no new tool dependency on the runner
- [x] No change to the clone, the formula rewrite, the validation, or the push

## Not in this PR

`Determine version tag` resolves a `workflow_run` trigger through `repos/.../releases/latest`, which skips prereleases. When the Release workflow's promote job had not yet flipped v0.26.0 to a full release, this job resolved **v0.25.0**, found the formula already up to date, and exited 0. A green run that moved nothing. Worth fixing, but it changes version-resolution behavior rather than adding a guard, so it belongs on its own.

body:
This change adds Slack notifications to alert approvers when a user requests the Contributor role via `eo pim`. The webhook URL is stored securely in Azure Key Vault rather than being committed to the repository.

## Summary

When a user runs `eo pim` to request the Contributor role, the CLI now posts a notification to Slack that includes:
- The requester's name and email
- The subscription and activation duration
- The justification (if provided)
- Links to approve via CLI or the Azure PIM portal

The notification is best-effort: if the webhook URL cannot be retrieved or Slack is unreachable, the command still succeeds and only reports that the notification was skipped.

## Key Changes

- **New `internal/slack` package**: Provides `Post()` to send messages to Slack incoming webhooks, with proper escaping of mrkdwn special characters and error handling that never leaks the webhook URL
- **New `internal/pim/notify.go`**: Implements `ActivationRequestedMessage()` to format the notification, `SlackWebhookURL()` to fetch the secret from Key Vault, and `NotifyActivationRequested()` to post it
- **Updated `cmd/eo/cmd_pim.go`**: Integrates notifications into the activation flow using background goroutines so Key Vault and Graph lookups overlap with the PIM request
- **Refactored user identity resolution**: Extracted `getSignedInUser()` helper in `cmd_helpers.go` to avoid duplication between `whoami` and PIM notification code
- **Updated help text and README**: Documents the Slack notification feature, setup instructions, and Key Vault requirements

## Summary

This adapts the immediately useful security work identified while reviewing Qortal PR #368 into Qortium Core's existing Zcash-family wallet architecture. It does not port the upstream PR wholesale or enable the Unified wallet.

- Load the configured Pirate wallet library from the exact immutable QDN transaction rather than following mutable name state.
- Serialize complete wallet-selected JNI operations through one bounded process-global lane.
- Fail closed until Core restart when a running native call times out or is interrupted with an uncertain outcome.
- Make the Pirate wallet controller lifecycle explicit and restartable after a clean stop.
- Return cached status while a long native operation owns the lane.
- Validate lightwallet chain identity and require corroborated server heights before permanently rejecting relative outliers.

## Security and compatibility details

- Full transaction signatures isolate native-library cache directories; older caches are retained.
- Only `LiteWalletJniAdapter` directly accesses the static JNI surface.
- Balance, list, address, key, seed, send, and P2SH flows keep wallet selection and native use in one atomic operation.
- NEW, STOPPING, TERMINATED, and DEGRADED controllers reject wallet operations.
- Clean controller shutdown consumes its stale wake-up interrupt only after the main loop exits; genuine interrupted in-flight native calls still degrade the lane before cleanup.
- Failed, null, invalid-info, wrong-chain, and rejected-height probes close their temporary gRPC channels.
- A malicious first height cannot poison the reference used for two honest agreeing servers.
- The wallet birthday floor is mainnet-only, so fresh TEST3/REGTEST probes remain usable.
- Existing endpoint paths and default response shapes are unchanged; no Home change is required.

## Validation

- Focused C1-C3 plus PirateChain gate: **62 tests**, 0 failures, 0 errors, 17 expected live-network skips.
- Post-CI-failure lifecycle/coordinator gate: **12 tests**, 0 failures, 0 errors.
- Fresh-JVM lifecycle stress: **100/100 runs passed**; the identical pre-fix loop failed on iteration 3.
- Full serialized suite: `mvn -DskipJUnitTests=false test`
  - **3,211 tests**, 0 failures, 0 errors, 67 skips
  - `BUILD SUCCESS` in 12:16
- `git diff --check origin/main..HEAD`
- Independent review confirmed that clearing the stale interrupt at the cleanup boundary preserves fail-closed behavior for genuinely interrupted JNI operations.
- Earlier review findings about stopped-controller work and non-mainnet birthday handling were fixed and regression-tested before the initial PR head.

## Out of scope

- Pirate Unified protobuf/JNI integration and migration
- Any QDN publication or native artifact replacement
- Home changes
- ARRR default enablement
- Deployment, release, or funded send/P2SH acceptance

Those remain separately gated because this code executes native wallet logic in-process and controls foreign-chain spending and trade settlement.

## Resumo

Add pure step-aggregation utils (daily/weekly/monthly) in src/utils/healthAggregation.ts

## Causa raiz

Não havia qualquer utilitário de agregação/data-bucketing em `src/utils/` (confirmado com `grep -rl "aggregate" src/utils/` — sem resultado). Qualquer trabalho futuro de gráfico/dashboard teria de duplicar a matemática de bucketing dentro de um componente (intestável sem render) ou saltá-la aos testes. O defeito é a ausência da função, não um sintoma num ecrã.

## O que mudou

- **`src/utils/healthAggregation.ts`** (novo): funções puras e sem dependências `aggregateDaily`, `aggregateWeekly`, `aggregateMonthly` mais os tipos `DailySteps` e `Bucket`.
  - Entrada não ordenada: `dedupeByDate` normaliza para um `Map<date, steps>` (preserva ordem, **última escrita ganha** em datas duplicadas — espelha o `HealthStore` que sobrepõe a entrada do dia).
  - `toBuckets` acumula `totalSteps` e `dayCount` por chave e ordena os buckets ascendente por `label`.
  - `dayCount` = dias **presentes** na entrada; `averageSteps = totalSteps / dayCount`, nunca diluído pelos dias de calendário sem dados.
  - `aggregateWeekly` usa `isoWeekKey` (ISO-8601, segunda-feira inicial) calculada em UTC para evitar deriva de DST. O ano da semana é o ano de **quinta-feira** da semana (ex.: sex 2027-01-01 → `2026-W53`).
  - `aggregateMonthly` agrupa por `'YYYY-MM'`.
  - As três devolvem `[]` para entrada vazia (sem lançar).
- **`src/utils/__tests__/healthAggregation.test.ts`** (novo): 17 testes, um ficheiro `describe`/`it` sem `render` (lógica pura com fixtures fixos, padrão referido no issue como `RemindersScreen.weekday.test.ts`).

## Porque assim

- ISO week: a primeira implementação usava `Math.floor(days/7)+1` a partir de 1 de janeiro, que ficava a semana errada (desfasamento de 1). Substituída pela fórmula ISO-8601 correcta (quinta-feira da semana define o ano-da-semana; primeira segunda-feira = 4 de janho ajustado). Verificada contra `date -d` do sistema para os casos-limite (2026-08-16 dom→W33; 2026-12-31 qui + 2027-01-01 sex→ambos W53).
- UTC em vez de local: os `Date` locais sofrem deriva de DST em redor de 1 de abril/outubro; como as datas são 'YYYY-MM-DD' sem hora, UTC mantém o dia estável.
- Não se tocou em nenhum store/screen — só se adicionou um ficheiro novo, como o issue exige. Zero `any`, zero `try/catch` a tapar erro.

## Critérios de aceitação

- [x] `aggregateDaily` devolve um bucket por data única, última escrita ganha em duplicados — testado (`returns one bucket per unique date...`).
- [x] `aggregateWeekly` agrupa por semana ISO (segunda inicial) e coloca um domingo na semana que começou na segunda anterior — testado (`buckets a Sunday into the week that started the preceding Monday`, 2026-08-16→W33).
- [x] `aggregateMonthly` agrupa por mês de calendário — testado (`groups by calendar month`).
- [x] `averageSteps` divide por `dayCount` (dias presentes), não pelo comprimento de calendário — testado nos três (`does not dilute average by calendar days...`).
- [x] Array vazio devolve `[]` para as três — testado (`returns [] for an empty input (no throw)` nos três `describe`).
- [x] Testes cobrem: entrada não ordenada, bucket sobre fronteira de mês (Ago→Set), fronteira de ano (31 Dez→1 Jan), datas duplicadas, e vazio — para as três funções.
- [x] O que NÃO devia mudar: nenhum ficheiro de store/screen foi tocado; nenhuma suite de teste alheia foi modificada nem posta `.skip`. Confirmado por `git status --porcelain` (só os dois ficheiros novos) e pela suite completa.

- **Passo vermelho:** antes de criar `healthAggregation.ts`, o teste foi corrido e falhou por não conseguir importar o módulo (o comportamento não existia):

```
FAIL Android src/utils/__tests__/healthAggregation.test.ts
```

body:
## Summary

Both `ghost-language/ghost` and `ghost-language/lumen` have moved substantially since this extension was last synced — most importantly, Ghost adopted an import-based module system (`import ... from "ghost:name"` / `"lumen:name"`) where only `console` and the global `type()` function remain reachable without an import. This PR brings the extension's data and providers up to date with both codebases (checked out and read directly, not guessed).

- **`src/api/ghost.js`** re-transcribed against the current interpreter:
  - The old `io` module split into `file` and `path`; the old `time` module is gone, folded into `os.sleep` and a new `date` module (date-fns-style, UTC only).
  - `math` grew enormously: trigonometry, a full linear-algebra layer, statistics, and arithmetic exposed as callable methods (127 members total).
  - `List` gained `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `sort`, `slice`, `concat`, `contains`, `reverse`, `unique`, `each`, and a new `shift()`. **`List.pop()` changed meaning** — it now pops from the end (mirroring `push`), and the old first-element behavior moved to `shift()`.
  - `Map` gained real methods (`get`, `set`, `has`, `keys`, `values`, `length`, `merge`) — previously undocumented as having none.
  - The global `print()` is gone entirely, replaced by `console.log`/`console.write`.
- **`src/api/lumen.js`** re-transcribed against the current engine:
  - Lumen no longer extends Ghost's `math` module at all — everything it used to bolt on there now ships natively in `ghost:math`.
  - `Image`, `Spritesheet`, `Animation`, `Source`, `Font`, `Target` and `Quad` are now `new`-able classes imported from their owning module (`lumen:image`, `lumen:audio`, `lumen:canvas`, `lumen:font`), replacing factory methods like the old `image.newSpritesheet()`/`canvas.newQuad()`.
- **`src/analyzer.js`** gained real import-statement parsing (`resolveImports`) supporting the bare, aliased, named (braced/unbraced), wildcard, and combined (`import name, { a, b } from "scheme:module"`) forms, plus `new Type(...)` assignment inference. All receiver/module resolution across the providers now goes through this instead of assuming every module name is globally available.
- **Completion, hover, signature help, and semantic highlighting** are now import-aware throughout: a module, alias, or named import only resolves (and only highlights) where the document actually imports it. Completion also now completes the `import` statement itself — module names after `import `, inside an open `"ghost:`/`"lumen:` string, and a module's members/classes inside `{ }` once the line names it via `from`.
- Extensive updates to `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, and `test/run.js` (now 123 checks, including a dedicated import-resolution suite) to match.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm test` — 123/123 passing
- [x] Manually verified the built API model against both source repos (module lists, method signatures, `List.pop()`/`shift()` semantics, `Map` methods, Lumen's class-vs-module split) via `node -e` smoke checks
- [ ] Manual smoke test in an Extension Development Host (not done in this sandboxed session — no VS Code UI available)

body:
At the end of a career the skill shop lists every buyable skill with its own hint discount, next to the trainee's stats and SP balance. Copying that out by hand is slow, and the hint levels are the part that decides what a plan costs.

`tools/career-export` reads it out of the running game with Frida and writes a `SkillPlannerExportData` JSON document, which a planner imports with no conversion step.

- `tools/career-export/career_export.py`: hooks `SingleModeSkillLearningViewController.BeginView` for the shop listing, and latches the career object from every no-arg getter on `WorkSingleModeData`. One hook is not enough. `WorkDataManager` exposes no static instance to walk to, the skill screen reads the chara from a reference it already holds, and 35 of those getters went uncalled across 12 seconds of a live client. When the pointer is still cold as `BeginView` fires the script says so and keeps waiting, rather than ending the run. It refuses to write a file when the read comes back incomplete, because zeroed stats look valid to whatever reads them next.
- `tools/career-export/README.md`: how to install and run it with `pip install frida` or with `uv`, which memory location each exported field comes from, and the offsets the shop listing uses.
- `tools/career-export/.gitignore`: an export describes a real account, so `*.json` and `*.log` stay out of the repository.
- `AGENTS.md`: the Rust-only boundary rule now allows `tools/`, which sits outside the Cargo workspace and which nothing inside it depends on.

Shop offsets and the IL2CPP class scan come from [UmaExtractor](https://github.com/xancia/UmaExtractor).

body:
## Summary
Adds `TaskMarketTool`, a new `smolagents.Tool` that lets a **human-operated** agent act as a [TaskMarket](https://taskmarket.dev) **requester**. TaskMarket is an on-chain (Base) agent task marketplace that escrows USDC before work begins, so workers are paid automatically on acceptance.

The tool supports four guarded actions:
- `configure` — lock the network to Base (`chain_id` 8453) and set a max spend (USDC).
- `create_task` — create + escrow a task. Requires `authorized_by_user=true` (fresh, explicit human authorization) and respects the spend cap.
- `get_status` — return the live task status (parsed JSON).
- `get_submissions` — return submissions for **human review** (never auto-accept/reject).

### Safety guarantees (per the integration requirement)
- **Network enforcement:** only Base (8453) is allowed; any other `chain_id` is rejected.
- **Spend cap:** `create_task` rejects rewards above the configured `max_spend_usdc`.
- **Fresh authorization:** `create_task` raises `PermissionError` unless `authorized_by_user` is `True` with an explicit human confirmation — no silent funding, no blind retry of unknown settlement.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** submissions are returned for review; the tool never decides acceptance/rejection.
- **No key handling:** private keys are never read, stored, logged, or committed. All on-chain actions are delegated to the first-party `taskmarket` CLI.

This target did not previously support Taskmarket and has not been submitted to earlier integration bounties.

## Setup instructions
```bash
npm install -g @lucid-agents/taskmarket
taskmarket init
```
The `taskmarket` binary must be on `PATH` (the tool falls back to `npx taskmarket`).

## Usage
```python
import json, time
from smolagents import TaskMarketTool

tool = TaskMarketTool()
tool.forward("configure", json.dumps({"max_spend_usdc": 50}))
tool.forward("create_task", json.dumps({
    "description": "Summarize the Q3 product roadmap as one markdown file.",
    "reward_usdc": 5,
    "deadline_unix": int(time.time()) + 7 * 86400,
    "deliverables": "one markdown file",
    "authorized_by_user": True,
}))
tool.forward("get_status", json.dumps({"task_id": "0x..."}))
tool.forward("get_submissions", json.dumps({"task_id": "0x..."}))
```

## Reproduction / tests
```bash
pytest tests/test_taskmarket.py
```
Local result: **13 passed**.
Tests cover: Base-only enforcement, spend-cap enforcement, required fresh authorization, micro-USDC reward conversion, task-id parsing, JSON status/submission parsing, unknown-action and invalid-JSON handling, and missing-CLI error messaging.

## Files
- `src/smolagents/taskmarket.py` — the `TaskMarketTool` implementation.
- `src/smolagents/__init__.py` — export the tool.
- `tests/test_taskmarket.py` — unit tests (mocked CLI).
- `docs/source/en/examples/taskmarket.md` — usage documentation.

## Related TaskMarket task
Submitted as the deliverable for TaskMarket task `TSK-4E4CXBM9` (merge-ready integration PR). Maintainer response / PR status: **open, unreviewed**.

## Checklist
- [x] Target is an established, actively maintained product that did not already support Taskmarket.
- [x] Public, non-draft PR against the official upstream repository.
- [x] Fresh explicit user authorization required before creating/funding a task.
- [x] Returns created task ID and live status; submissions presented for human review.
- [x] Network + spending checks enforced; no blind payment retry.
- [x] No private keys requested/stored/logged/committed.
- [x] Meaningful automated tests + docs + reproduction commands.

## What does this PR do?

Caps the Anthropic `max` thinking variant's `budgetTokens` to `⌊model.limit.output / 2 − 1⌋` (mirroring the existing `high` variant's half-output discipline), so the derived `max_tokens` always strictly exceeds `budget_tokens`.

## Why?

Anthropic's API requires `0 < budget_tokens < max_tokens`. The previous `max` variant used `budgetTokens: Math.min(31_999, model.limit.output - 1)`. For any model whose output limit is ≤ 31_999 — e.g. the common 8_192 / 16_384 default-output Claude models — that made `budget_tokens` equal `output - 1`, while `maxOutputTokens()` derives `max_tokens = modelCap - budgetTokens`, collapsing `max_tokens` to `1`. That violates `budget_tokens < max_tokens` and the request fails with an HTTP 400 before any work happens.

On large-output models (> ~64k output) the `31_999` floor still keeps the `max` budget above `high`, so high-throughput models are unaffected.

## How was it tested?

- New regression guard in `packages/synergy/test/provider/transform.test.ts`: a `test.each` over `[8192, 16384, 32000, 64000]` asserts both `high` and `max` satisfy `0 < budget_tokens < max_tokens` (where `max_tokens` is derived from the same budget via `ProviderTransform.maxOutputTokens`).
- Updated the existing output-8192 expectation: the `max` budget is now `4095` (was `8191`).

body:
## Problem

- A short Redis outage broke every AI observability ClickHouse query at once, instead of only the ones that needed a concurrency slot.
- `RateLimit.use()` ran its Lua script through `redis eval` with no error handling, so a Redis socket timeout escaped the limiter and failed the query.
- That call sits under `_llm_analytics_concurrency_slot`, which wraps every query tagged `ClickHouseUser.LLM_ANALYTICS`: the AI observability Temporal activities, `query_ai_events`, and `TraceQueryRunner`. One Redis blip failed all of them and fanned out into many distinct error tracking issues.

## Changes

- The limiter now runs the query when Redis is unavailable, rather than failing it. `use()` and `release()` catch `RedisError` and fail open by returning the existing `None` bypass.
- A failed `release()` is safe: the slot still expires through its TTL, so it only leaks briefly.
- A new counter, `posthog_clickhouse_query_concurrency_limiter_redis_error`, records each fail-open by `limit_name` and `operation`, so the bypass is visible.
- The LLM analytics limiter gets a 3s per-call Redis socket timeout, so a stalled call fails open fast instead of blocking for the global 20s default, which the limiter's own 10s `retry_timeout` already exceeds.
- Mechanical: `redis.get_client()` takes an optional `socket_timeout` and caches one client per distinct timeout.

## How did you test this code?

- Added two cases to `TestRateLimit`. They catch a regression that no existing test did: removing the `try/except` would let a Redis error escape `use()` or `release()` again.
  - `test_use_fails_open_when_redis_errors`: a `RedisError` from `eval` returns `None` and counts the bypass, rather than raising.
  - `test_release_swallows_redis_error`: a `RedisError` from `zrem` does not raise and counts the bypass.
- Ran `posthog/clickhouse/client/test/test_limit.py::TestRateLimit` locally: all cases pass.
- Not run: the wider ClickHouse-backed suites, because this change is scoped to the limiter.

None. No user-facing behavior, API, or documented workflow changes.

**Autonomy:** Fully autonomous

- Authored by an agent (Claude Code) from an inbox report about the Redis timeout burst.
- Skills invoked: `/writing-tests`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`, `/writing-code-comments`, `/writing-user-facing-copy`, `/writing-simplified-technical-english`.
- The fix follows the report's recommendation: catch `RedisError`, count it, fail open, and tighten the per-call socket timeout for this limiter.
